ὅρμ-ημα , ατος, τό,
A.sudden rush, swoop, onset,
“ἀετοῦ”
LXX De. 28.49
; of attacking troops, ib. 1 Ma. 4.8 , al.; of the fall of a stone, Apoc. 18.21 : pl., rapid movement, ὁρμήμασι νηός,
= νηῒ ὁρμωμένη , Orac. ap. Ael. NA 13.21 .
2.
= ὁρμή , impulse, incitement, motive,
“μηδ᾽ . . ἡμῶν τι συνεργὸν μηδ᾽ ὅ.”
Epicur. Nat. 98
G., cf. Plu. 2.452c ; τὸ ὅ. μου my indignation,
LXX Ho. 5.10 ; θαλάσσης -ήματα, of the tides, Procl. Par.Ptol. 4 .
II. the earliest ex. is “Ἑλένης ὁρμήματά τε στοναχάς τε”
Il. 2.356
, 590 , where Ἑλένης is taken by Aristarch. ap. Sch.A as the objective gen., the cares (as if from ὁρμαίνω) and groans [of the Greeks] about Helen, i. e. caused by her; by the χωρίζοντες (ibid.) as the subjective gen., the searchings of heart and groans of Helen ; the former view is more prob., but ὁ. may be from ὁρμάομαι and mean the rushes, struggles of war.
From A Greek-English Lexicon (Henry George Liddell, Robert Scott, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1940)
